title: AI + Vendors Case Study 2026: Property Management Glossary
body_text: TL;DR An AI + vendors case study documents how an AI tool performed in a real property management deployment, with named metrics, timelines, and integration details. Property managers face a unique challenge: “vendor” means both the AI software company and the maintenance contractors AI dispatches. This glossary defines every term you’ll encounter during AI vendor demos and evaluations, explains how to spot cherry-picked case studies, and provides a framework for measuring real ROI against industry benchmarks. Quick Answer: What Is an AI + Vendors Case Study? An AI + vendors case study in property management is a documented report showing how an AI system performed during a real-world deployment. A credible case study should include: Element What to Look For Company name Named property management company Portfolio size Number of units managed PMS integration Which property management software was connected Timeline Deployment duration Baseline metrics Before-deployment performance Outcome metrics Response times, containment rates, cost reductions Service vendor coordination Maintenance dispatch performance Compliance Fair Housing and regulatory safeguards The term "vendor" has two meanings in property management AI: The AI software company selling the technology. The maintenance contractors performing repair work. Strong case studies evaluate both. Bottom line: If a case study doesn't include baseline metrics, implementation timelines, integration details, and documented outcomes, treat it as marketing rather than evidence. Why Property Managers Need This Glossary When you sit through an AI vendor demo, the word “vendor” does double duty. The sales rep is the vendor. The plumber your AI dispatches at 2 AM is also a vendor. No one clarifies which meaning they’re using, and that ambiguity creates real confusion during evaluations, contract negotiations, and case study reviews. This is not a trivial semantic point. A NARPM survey found property managers spend roughly 40% of their time on tenant communications, with maintenance requests making up the largest share. AI tools promise to compress that time dramatically. But evaluating whether those promises hold up requires understanding the vocabulary. The pages that currently rank for “AI + vendors case study” cover enterprise deployments at companies like AWS and ServiceNow. None address property management. None distinguish between the two meanings of “vendor” that matter to your business. This glossary fills that gap. Explore Haven’s maintenance AI to see how these concepts work in practice. The Two Types of “Vendor” in Property Management AI Before defining individual terms, this distinction needs to be clear because it affects everything that follows. AI technology vendor refers to the software company selling you an AI product. EliseAI, Haven, Vendoroo, and similar companies fall into this category. When someone says “vendor case study,” they usually mean a documented deployment story published by one of these companies. Maintenance/service vendor refers to the plumber, HVAC technician, electrician, or general contractor you dispatch for repairs. AI-powered vendor dispatch automates the assignment, notification, and follow-up with these contractors. Both types of vendors show up in AI + vendors case studies for property management. A strong case study should address both: how well the AI technology vendor’s product performed, and how effectively it coordinated your service vendors. Keep this distinction in mind as you work through the terms below. AI Vendor vs. Maintenance Vendor Category AI Technology Vendor Maintenance Service Vendor Primary role Provides AI software Performs repairs Examples AI maintenance platforms Plumbers, electricians, HVAC contractors Relationship Technology partnership Service partnership Success metric AI performance Work completion Typical contract Software agreement Service agreement Measured through Containment, ROI, CSAT Resolution time, repair quality This distinction is critical because most AI case studies discuss technology vendors while property managers spend most of their time coordinating maintenance vendors. Property Management AI Metrics Cheat Sheet These are the metrics that appear most frequently in AI vendor case studies. Metric Good Question to Ask Why It Matters Containment rate How many requests were resolved without staff involvement? Measures automation effectiveness Deflection rate How many requests never reached a human? Measures workload reduction Time-to-resolution How long did maintenance take from start to finish? Measures operational efficiency Cost per ticket How much does each maintenance request cost? Measures financial performance CSAT How satisfied were tenants? Measures service quality ROI Did savings exceed implementation costs? Measures investment performance Payback period How quickly were costs recovered? Measures implementation success When comparing vendors, prioritize containment rate and time-to-resolution over vanity metrics such as chatbot interactions or total conversations handled. AI Vendor Evaluation Terms These are the terms you’ll encounter when comparing AI technology vendors and reading their published case studies. AI Vendor Case Study A documented account of an AI deployment at a named company, including the problem, solution, implementation details, and measurable results. The key word is “documented.” A testimonial quote on a homepage is not a case study. A proper AI + vendors case study names the company, discloses the portfolio size, specifies which systems were integrated, and provides before-and-after metrics. The catch: published case studies skew positive because vendors publish wins, not stalled rollouts. Savings are often credited to the tool when a broader transformation (new processes, better staffing, cleaner data) deserves much of the credit. For a real example of what a property management case study looks like with actual metrics, see this AI call center case study . Proof of Concept (PoC) A limited test of an AI vendor’s tool using your real data and workflows. Unlike a demo, a PoC runs against actual maintenance requests or leasing inquiries from your portfolio. It typically lasts two to four weeks and tests whether the AI can handle your specific property types, tenant demographics, and PMS configuration. A PoC answers one question: does this work with our data? It does not answer whether it will work at scale. For guidance on what to expect during this phase, the AI implementation timeline guide breaks down each stage. Pilot Program A controlled rollout to a subset of your portfolio before full deployment. If you manage 1,200 units, you might pilot across 200 units for 60 to 90 days. Pilots surface integration issues, edge cases in triage logic, and vendor dispatch failures that a PoC’s limited scope would miss. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr, who has deployed over 20 AI agents across his operations, recommends this approach strongly. His advice: “Pick one or two vendors. Train them deeply. Commit for 90 days. Make an informed decision based on real results from properly trained agents.” Running simultaneous bake-offs across multiple vendors, by contrast, produces shallow results. Vendor SLA (Service Level Agreement) A contractual commitment from the AI technology vendor specifying performance guarantees. This includes uptime percentages, response time thresholds, accuracy targets, and escalation protocols when the system fails. Three related terms cause frequent confusion: SLI (Service Level Indicator) : The actual measured metric, like “average call answer time was 4.2 seconds.” SLO (Service Level Objective) : The internal target, like “we aim to answer calls within 5 seconds.” SLA (Service Level Agreement) : The contractual guarantee with penalties if the SLO is missed. SLAs matter enormously in property management because regulatory liability stays with you , not your AI vendor. One property management company using an AI platform reached a $45,000 settlement with the state of Pennsylvania after the attorney general found the company failed to maintain safe housing. The AI vendor didn’t get the lawsuit. The property manager did. Vendor Lock-In The risk of becoming dependent on a single AI platform to the point where switching costs become prohibitive. Lock-in happens when an AI vendor stores your data in proprietary formats, when custom integrations are built on non-standard APIs, or when years of training data and conversation history can’t be exported. To evaluate lock-in risk, ask during demos: Can we export our data? What format? What happens to our PMS integrations if we leave? Build vs. Buy The decision framework for whether to develop AI capabilities in-house or purchase from an established vendor. For property management companies managing 350 to 2,000 units, building custom AI is almost never practical. The cost of hiring ML engineers, maintaining models, and keeping up with PMS API changes dwarfs the license fees of purpose-built solutions. The build path only makes sense for the largest REITs with dedicated engineering teams and portfolios exceeding 50,000 units. Bake-Off Testing multiple AI vendors simultaneously on the same workflows. While the concept sounds logical, practitioners report significant downsides. Each vendor needs training data, configuration time, and staff attention. Splitting those resources across three or four vendors means none gets trained properly. Results reflect the shallow setup, not the tool’s actual capability. Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) The full cost of an AI deployment including license fees, implementation, PMS integration, staff training, workflow redesign, and ongoing maintenance. This is where most budgets go sideways. Ron Ash, CEO of Accenture Federal Services, has quantified this gap: for every $1 spent on AI technology, organizations must invest $9 in change management, workforce training, and workflow redesign. Vendors almost never include that ratio in their published cost models. When you read an AI + vendors case study that claims 300% ROI, ask whether the $9 is accounted for. AI-Powered Vendor Dispatch and Coordination Terms These terms describe how AI handles the coordination of your maintenance and service vendors, the other kind of vendor in your daily operations. Vendor Dispatch Automation AI automatically receiving maintenance requests, assigning the best-fit contractor, notifying them, scheduling the work, and updating work orders, all without manual phone calls or emails. This is the most operationally complex AI use case in property management and the one with the highest liability if it fails. Consider a realistic scenario: a tenant reports a water leak at 2:17 AM. The AI triages it as high priority, identifies the on-call plumber from the preferred vendor list, dispatches them, and notifies the tenant, all within minutes. No property manager wakes up. For a deeper walkthrough of this workflow, see how AI vendor dispatch works . Industry data shows average maintenance response time drops from 4.6 days to under 18 hours within 30 days of implementing automated dispatch systems. Preferred Vendor List A curated roster of approved contractors organized by trade, location, availability, and cost that the AI uses when dispatching. This is the foundation of vendor dispatch automation. If your preferred vendor list contains outdated phone numbers, retired contractors, or missing trade categories, the AI will faithfully dispatch to a dead end. Explore Haven’s AI maintenance coordinator to see how preferred vendor lists integrate with automated dispatch. Best practice: audit your preferred vendor list quarterly. Verify contact information, confirm insurance and licensing status, and update availability windows. The AI follows your rules, so the rules need to be current. Vendor Matching The algorithm-based assignment of a work order to a specific contractor based on trade specialty, geographic proximity, current availability, historical performance ratings, and sometimes cost history. More sophisticated systems also factor in tenant preferences and vendor response time patterns. Emergency Triage AI classification of incoming maintenance requests by severity level. The standard tiers are life-safety (gas leak, fire, flooding), urgent (no heat in winter, broken lock), and routine (dripping faucet, cosmetic damage). The AI’s triage accuracy determines whether emergencies get the immediate response they require or sit in a queue. Property management AI systems report that 65% of calls arrive outside standard business hours, making automated triage essential. For detailed triage logic and escalation workflows, the AI escalation rules glossary explains each tier and how escalation triggers work. Escalation Rules The conditions that trigger human involvement or immediate vendor dispatch. Examples include: any request classified as life-safety escalates to the on-call property manager immediately, any vendor who hasn’t confirmed acceptance within 15 minutes triggers reassignment to the backup contractor, or any tenant who calls back about the same issue within 48 hours escalates for manager review. Work Order Automation AI creating, updating, and closing work orders directly inside your property management system. This goes beyond just logging a request. Full work order automation means the AI writes the work order with the correct property, unit, issue category, and priority level, then updates it as the vendor confirms, arrives, and completes the work, then closes it after a follow-up with the tenant confirms resolution. Containment Rate The percentage of maintenance requests the AI resolves without any human intervention. If your AI handles 1,000 requests in a month and 700 are fully resolved (triaged, dispatched, completed, followed up, and closed) without a property manager touching them, your containment rate is 70%. This is arguably the single most important metric in any property management AI + vendors case study. High containment rates translate directly to staff time savings and cost reduction. Vendor Follow-Up Automated post-repair check-ins with tenants to confirm the issue was resolved satisfactorily. This step is frequently overlooked in manual workflows but significantly impacts tenant satisfaction and renewal rates. AI follow-ups typically happen via SMS or phone call 24 to 48 hours after the work order is marked complete. Case Study and ROI Measurement Terms These terms appear in the results sections of AI vendor case studies. Understanding them helps you separate genuine performance data from marketing. Baseline Metrics Pre-deployment performance data that establishes the “before” in any before-and-after comparison. Common baselines in property management include average time-to-resolution for maintenance requests, cost per ticket, tenant satisfaction scores, after-hours response rates, and vacancy duration. Without documented baselines, an AI + vendors case study cannot prove anything. If a case study claims “50% faster response times” but doesn’t specify what the response time was before deployment, the number is meaningless. For guidance on ensuring your data is clean enough to establish reliable baselines, see this AI data quality guide . ROI (Return on Investment) Revenue gained or costs saved relative to the total AI investment. Simple formula: (Gains from AI minus Cost of AI) divided by Cost of AI, expressed as a percentage. Industry benchmarks vary widely. Companies investing in AI-powered customer service see average returns of $3.50 for every $1 spent, with leading organizations achieving up to 8x. For agentic AI specifically, companies report an average ROI of 171%, with U.S. enterprises hitting 192%. But here’s the critical caveat. According to Gartner’s 2024 AI Implementation Outlook, the gap between projected and realized AI ROI in enterprise deployments is consistently 30 to 40%. That gap is rarely disclosed in vendor materials. For property management specific ROI analysis, the AI benefits, use cases, and ROI guide provides more grounded benchmarks. Payback Period The time required to recoup your AI deployment costs through savings or revenue gains. First-year returns in AI customer service deployments average 41%, climbing to 87% in year two and exceeding 124% by year three as systems learn from real interactions. Property management deployments typically show faster payback on maintenance AI than leasing AI because the cost savings (reduced after-hours staffing, fewer unnecessary dispatches) are more immediately measurable. Deflection Rate The percentage of inquiries handled entirely by AI without routing to a human agent. Different from containment rate in an important way: deflection measures initial handling, while containment measures end-to-end resolution. An AI might deflect 90% of calls (it answers them) but only contain 60% (the rest eventually need human follow-up). Resolution Rate The percentage of issues AI resolves completely from start to finish. In maintenance contexts, resolution means the problem is fixed, the work order is closed, and the tenant confirms satisfaction. In leasing contexts, resolution might mean the prospect books a tour or submits an application. CSAT (Customer Satisfaction Score) Tenant satisfaction with AI interactions, typically measured through post-interaction surveys on a 1 to 5 scale. CSAT is often the metric that surprises property managers most. Tenants frequently rate AI interactions higher than human ones because the AI responds instantly, is available at 2 AM, and never sounds annoyed. Cost Per Ticket Total support cost divided by the number of tickets handled. This includes staff time, vendor coordination overhead, phone system costs, and AI license fees. An effective AI deployment should measurably reduce cost per ticket. If a case study doesn’t disclose this number, the vendor either didn’t track it or didn’t like the result. Time-to-Resolution Duration from when a tenant submits a request to when the issue is fully resolved. For property management, this is measured in hours or days, not minutes. AI’s biggest impact on time-to-resolution comes from eliminating delays in the intake and dispatch phases, not from making the plumber work faster. AI-powered maintenance systems can achieve up to a 25% reduction in unnecessary technician dispatches through better triage and troubleshooting, which compresses the overall resolution timeline for the requests that do need on-site work. Silent Degradation An AI system performing poorly without visible errors, crashes, or alerts. This term comes from real deployment experience. Jason Lemkin described one production AI agent that “quietly stopped ingesting new training data. No error message. No alert. No crash. It just kept running on an increasingly stale knowledge base for four months.” For property managers, silent degradation might look like an AI that still answers calls and creates work orders, but gradually becomes less accurate at triage because it stopped learning from new interactions months ago. Regular QA reviews catch silent degradation. Trusting the system’s uptime dashboard does not. The ROI Gap The difference between what an AI vendor projects during the sales process and what the deployment actually delivers. Gartner pegs this gap at 30 to 40% for enterprise AI deployments. The gap exists because vendor projections assume optimal data quality, rapid adoption by staff, and smooth integrations, none of which describe a typical property management deployment. According to Gartner, organizations that pursue end-to-end AI integration achieve cost savings up to 25%, while those running isolated AI experiments see 5% or less. The depth of your commitment determines which side of the ROI gap you land on. How to Compare Two AI Vendor Case Studies Never compare AI case studies based on ROI percentages alone. Use this framework instead: Comparison Factor Vendor A Vendor B Portfolio size Unit count PMS integration Implementation timeline Containment rate Time-to-resolution First-year ROI Payback period Fair Housing testing Two vendors reporting identical ROI numbers may have achieved those results under completely different operating conditions. Always normalize results by portfolio size, property type, and implementation depth. How to Read an AI Vendor Case Study: A 5-Point Framework Not all case studies are created equal. Use this checklist when reviewing any AI + vendors case study, especially those from property management AI companies. 1. Is the company named? Anonymous case studies (“a mid-size property management firm”) are marketing, not evidence. Named companies with disclosed unit counts allow you to verify and contextualize the results. 2. Are the metrics specific and verifiable? Hard data is the best way to gauge success. Look for case studies that include specific percentages, dollar savings, or time reductions. “Significant improvement” is not a metric. “Response time dropped from 4.6 days to 18 hours” is. 3. Is integration depth disclosed? A strong case study will explain how the AI solution connected to existing systems. Which PMS? Read-only or read-write access? Were work orders created automatically or just logged? Superficial integration produces superficial results. 4. Are challenges and timelines included? Any case study that reads like pure success is almost certainly cherry-picked. Honest deployments involve configuration issues, staff resistance, data cleanup, and ramp-up periods. If a case study doesn’t mention any of these, it’s leaving out the parts that matter most for your planning. 5. Is Fair Housing compliance addressed? For property management specifically, any AI + vendors case study should confirm the system was tested for Fair Housing compliance . AI that treats tenant requests differently based on protected characteristics creates legal exposure that no ROI justifies. Five AI Vendor Red Flags Research from the AI For Real podcast and practitioner communities identifies these warning signs during evaluation: Lack of transparency about methodology and data. If the vendor can’t explain how their model works, what data it trains on, and how it handles edge cases, walk away. Vague or unverifiable performance metrics. “Our AI resolves 95% of requests” means nothing without definitions of what counts as “resolved” and how it was measured. Limited support and maintenance commitments. Post-sale support predicts long-term success. Lemkin’s team rejected two leading AI vendors “not because their products weren’t good, but because their sales teams couldn’t explain deployment details or fought against our requirements.” Sales team quality predicts post-sale success. Poor or non-existent documentation. If the vendor can’t provide technical documentation, integration guides, and troubleshooting protocols before you sign, they won’t magically appear after. Overemphasis on hype over practical application. Watch for vendors who spend more time talking about “transformative AI” and less time explaining how their system handles a backed-up toilet at midnight. What Property Managers Should Ask During AI Vendor Demos Armed with this vocabulary, here are five questions that separate serious AI vendors from marketing machines: “Can you show me a case study from a property management company managing a similar number of units to mine, with named metrics?” This question alone eliminates most weak vendors. “What is your containment rate across your property management deployments, and how do you measure it?” Containment rate is the metric that matters most. If they can’t answer, they either don’t track it or don’t want to share it. “What does your SLA guarantee for after-hours emergency triage accuracy?” If there’s no SLA for accuracy, there’s no accountability. “What is the total cost of ownership for the first year, including integration, training, and change management?” Remember the 9:1 rule. For every $1 in technology, plan for $9 in everything else. A vendor who only quotes the license fee is hiding the real cost. “What happens to my data if I cancel?” This reveals vendor lock-in risk and data portability, both critical for long-term flexibility. The biggest mistake in AI vendor selection, according to practitioners who’ve been through the process, is evaluating vendors before defining what success looks like for your firm. Without clear use cases and ROI metrics, you end up comparing features instead of outcomes. See how Haven’s AI property management software approaches these questions with transparent deployment practices and PMS integration. How to Choose an AI Vendor for Property Management Follow this evaluation process: Step 1: Define Your Use Case Determine whether your primary goal is: Maintenance automation Leasing automation Tenant communications Vendor dispatch After-hours call handling Step 2: Establish Baseline Metrics Measure: Current response times Cost per maintenance ticket After-hours call volume Tenant satisfaction Step 3: Run a Proof of Concept Test the AI using real maintenance requests and real tenant conversations. Step 4: Launch a Pilot Program Deploy the system to a small portion of your portfolio before expanding. Step 5: Measure Results Against Baselines Compare actual performance against: Containment rate Time-to-resolution Cost per ticket ROI Never choose an AI vendor based solely on a product demonstration. Frequently Asked Questions What is an AI + vendors case study in property management? It’s a documented account of how an AI tool performed in a real property management deployment. A strong case study names the company, discloses portfolio size, specifies which PMS was integrated, and provides before-and-after metrics for things like response time, cost per ticket, and containment rate. It should address both the AI technology vendor’s performance and how effectively the system coordinated maintenance service vendors. Why do AI vendor case studies often overstate ROI? Vendors publish wins, not failures. Gartner’s research shows a consistent 30 to 40% gap between projected and realized AI ROI. Additionally, published case studies typically credit savings entirely to the AI tool when broader changes (process redesign, better staffing, cleaner data) contributed significantly. Always ask whether the TCO includes the full implementation cost, not just the license fee. How do I evaluate whether an AI vendor’s case study is credible? Check five things: Is the company named? Are the metrics specific and verifiable? Is the PMS integration depth described? Are challenges and implementation timelines disclosed? And for property management, is Fair Housing compliance addressed? If any of these are missing, treat the case study with skepticism. What is silent degradation in AI systems? Silent degradation occurs when an AI system performs poorly without generating errors or alerts. The system stays “on” but produces increasingly inaccurate results. In property management, this might mean maintenance requests are being triaged incorrectly or vendor dispatches are going to the wrong contractors, all without any visible warning. Regular QA audits are the only reliable way to catch it. What containment rate should I expect from property management AI? Containment rate varies by deployment depth and portfolio complexity. The industry data suggests that AI-powered maintenance systems can resolve a significant majority of routine requests without human intervention, while complex or life-safety issues appropriately escalate. Ask any vendor for their portfolio-wide average and their range across different property types. How much does it actually cost to implement AI in property management? The license fee is typically a small fraction of the total. Using the 9:1 framework (for every $1 in tech, budget $9 for change management, training, data cleanup, and workflow redesign), a $2,000 monthly AI license translates to roughly $18,000 in implementation support over the first year. Companies that budget only for the software consistently fall short of projected ROI. What’s the difference between a pilot program and a proof of concept? A proof of concept tests whether the AI works with your data, usually over two to four weeks with limited scope. A pilot program is a controlled rollout across a subset of your portfolio (say 200 of 1,200 units) for 60 to 90 days. The PoC answers “can it work?” The pilot answers “will it work at scale?” Both should happen before full deployment.

title: How Long Does an IRS Refund Take? (2026 Timeline)
summary: How long an IRS tax refund takes in 2026 - 21 days for most e-filed returns with direct deposit, 6–8 weeks for paper filings, up to 20 weeks for amended returns.
body_text: Most federal tax refunds arrive within 21 days of e-filing when taxpayer chooses direct deposit IRS's stated processing goal for standard, error-free returns. Paper returns take substantially longer, typically 6 to 8 weeks . Amended returns (Form 1040-X) can take up to 20 weeks to process. Those are headline numbers. What actually happens between filing and refund is more nuanced. Here is complete 2026 refund timeline, what causes delays, how to check status, and what "still processing" really means when it drags past 21-day mark. The IRS refund timeline in 2026 The IRS reports that more than 90% of refunds are issued in less than 21 days for taxpayers who electronically file and select direct deposit. That statistic assumes: The return is complete and accurate The taxpayer's identity does not require additional verification The return does not claim Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) or Additional Child Tax Credit (ACTC) those are subject to a longer statutory hold No IRS backlog issues at specific processing center Here is practical refund timeline by filing method: Filing method Typical refund window E-file + direct deposit 8–21 days E-file + paper check 3–4 weeks Paper file + direct deposit 4–8 weeks Paper file + paper check 6–8 weeks Amended return (Form 1040-X) Up to 20 weeks The fastest combination is always e-file plus direct deposit . Paper filing at any stage adds weeks. What can delay your refund If your refund is running past 21-day mark, one of following is usually cause. EITC or ACTC on your return. Under Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act, IRS is required by law to hold refunds claiming Earned Income Tax Credit or Additional Child Tax Credit until at least February 15 each year. This is a fraud-prevention rule IRS uses extra time to match employer W-2 filings against reported wages. Practically, most PATH-Act-affected refunds land by last week of February or first week of March. Errors or math discrepancies. If numbers on return do not match IRS records (wages, withholding, dependents), return gets flagged for manual review. This can add 2–8 weeks to processing. Identity verification. The IRS increasingly requires taxpayers to verify identity through IRS ID Verification if return is flagged by fraud filter. This adds 2–9 weeks depending on how quickly taxpayer responds. Refund offset. If taxpayer owes past-due federal or state taxes, child support, or defaulted student loans, Treasury Offset Program automatically reduces refund before payment. The taxpayer receives a notice explaining offset. Injured spouse allocation (Form 8379). When one spouse's tax obligations trigger a refund offset that affects other spouse's share, injured spouse can file Form 8379 to claim their portion. This adds up to 14 weeks to processing. Amended returns. Form 1040-X returns are processed manually rather than through automated e-file system. Current IRS wait time is up to 20 weeks sometimes longer during high-volume periods. How to check your refund status The IRS provides three official ways to check refund status. Do not use third-party apps or SMS services that claim to offer faster updates they are pulling from same IRS API on same schedule. Where's My Refund tool. Available at IRS.gov/refunds . Updates once per day, usually overnight. Requires three inputs: Social Security Number (or ITIN), filing status, and exact refund amount from return. IRS2Go mobile app. Same data source as Where's My Refund, mobile-friendly interface. Available for iOS and Android. Amended return status. Amended returns use a separate tool: "Where's My Amended Return?" at IRS.gov. Status appears 3 weeks after filing and covers up to 3 tax years back. Status availability: E-file: 24 hours after IRS accepts return Paper file: 4 weeks after IRS receives mailed return Amended: 3 weeks after filing What "still processing" means The most common status past 21-day mark is "Return received" or "Still processing." This does not automatically mean something is wrong. Common reasons for "still processing" beyond 21 days: The return is under identity verification review The return is subject to PATH Act hold (EITC/ACTC) The return contains a schedule that requires manual review (large business losses, Schedule C with high deductions, first-year home office, unusual credits) The taxpayer filed late in season and IRS is running a backlog The IRS made an adjustment (usually smaller than expected refund) that requires a notice When to actually call IRS: The IRS asks taxpayers not to call about refund status until: More than 21 days have passed since e-filing More than 6 weeks have passed since paper filing The Where's My Refund tool specifically instructs you to call The IRS Refund Hotline is 1-800-829-1954. Wait times are longest February through April. How to get your refund faster next year Filing choices that reliably shorten refund timing: File electronically. Every study on refund timing shows e-file cuts processing by weeks. Choose direct deposit. Paper checks add 2–3 weeks over direct deposit. File early. Late January to mid-February is sweet spot. Filing in March or April means competing with peak-season backlog. Double-check your return. Common errors wrong SSN, wrong filing status, math mistakes, missing signatures on paper returns trigger manual review. Match your W-2s exactly. The IRS cross-references reported wages against employer filings. Rounding or transcription errors cause holds. Split your refund across accounts (Form 8888) if that fits. This does not slow processing. For small business owners, clean bookkeeping matters more than most realize. Returns that reconcile cleanly to books (Schedule C, Schedule E, K-1s) rarely trigger deeper audit filters. Returns where deductions look inconsistent with reported income often result of messy bookkeeping and reconciliation during year get flagged more often. Amended returns: exception to everything above Amended returns (Form 1040-X) do not follow 21-day timeline. Per IRS, current amended return processing takes up to 20 weeks sometimes longer. Why amended returns take so long: They are processed manually rather than through automated e-file pipeline Every amended return requires a human reviewer The IRS staffing on amended returns has not scaled with volume Amended returns often trigger secondary review (schedule C changes, credit claims, entity elections) Practical advice: file amended returns only when necessary. If a client discovers an error mid-year, waiting for an amended refund can mean waiting until following spring. This is one reason CPAs pay careful attention to Q4 tax planning catching issues before original return goes out is materially faster than fixing them afterward. FAQ How long does IRS take to deposit a refund? For e-filed returns with direct deposit selected, IRS's stated goal is 21 days or less. About 90% of refunds meet this window. Paper checks add 2–3 weeks. Why is my refund taking longer than 21 days? The most common causes are PATH Act hold (EITC/ACTC), identity verification, math or transcription errors, IRS backlog, refund offset, or a return schedule that requires manual review. How can I speed up my IRS refund? You cannot speed up a refund already in processing. For next year: e-file, choose direct deposit, file early in season, and double-check return before submitting. How long does an amended tax return take? Up to 20 weeks per current IRS processing time. Some amended returns take longer during high-volume periods. Check status at "Where's My Amended Return?" on IRS.gov, available 3 weeks after filing. What does "Return received" status mean? The IRS has received and accepted your return but has not yet issued refund. This is normal status for first 1–3 weeks of processing on e-filed returns. What does "Still processing" mean? The return is past initial acceptance stage but refund has not been issued. Common when return is under identity verification, subject to PATH Act hold, or flagged for manual review of a specific schedule. Not automatically a problem. When should I call IRS about my refund? The IRS asks taxpayers to wait 21 days after e-filing or 6 weeks after paper filing before calling. The Refund Hotline is 1-800-829-1954. Does state refund follow federal timeline? No. Each state runs its own refund processing on its own schedule, ranging from 1–3 weeks in fast states to 8–12 weeks in slower ones. Check your state Department of Revenue's refund tracker for status. Conclusion 21 days is IRS's target for most e-filed refunds with direct deposit. Paper filings and amended returns take substantially longer. If your refund is past that window, delay is almost always one of a small set of causes PATH Act hold, ID verification, math error, offset, or manual review and Where's My Refund at IRS.gov tells you which. Refund Delayed by Messy Books? Clean AI-native bookkeeping on QuickBooks and Xero accurate returns, fewer flags, faster refunds. Free for your first entity. Start Free

title: Furniture Delivery for Interior Designers: Getting Every Vendor's Piece There on Install Day
summary: The dozen vendor deliveries before install day are what eat a project's margin. When to rent a warehouse, and when to route instead.
body_text: Install day is where a design project's margin gets made or eaten, and what eats it is usually the dozen deliveries that come before the final one. A receiving warehouse is the right tool when pieces ship by freight over weeks and the client's site can't take a single carton yet. On a locally sourced, quick-turn room it's mostly storage you're renting for furniture that could have moved the day it was ready. Lugg is an on-demand moving and delivery service that can consolidate pickups from up to five vendors into a single route, which fits designers sourcing locally on a compressed install timeline. It covers more than 4,000 cities and 8,000 ZIP codes, so a project's sourcing radius rarely decides the answer. The U.S. interior design industry runs about $26.4 billion in 2026 , and a real slice of that revenue leaks out coordinating deliveries no one built a system to catch. One project pulls pieces from a to-the-trade vendor, two local showrooms, a marketplace find, and a custom workroom, each arriving on its own schedule with nowhere central to land. The default fix the industry sells is a receiving warehouse. It's the right tool for some projects and overkill for others. Here's how designers decide which they need — and how they pull a scattered vendor list into a single route when a warehouse isn't the answer. Receiving Warehouse vs. Multi-Stop Route: Which Fits the Project Most of the delivery decision comes down to how a project is sourced and how long pieces sit before they're installed. Project profile Receiving warehouse Multi-stop route Custom, to-the-trade, freight-shipped over weeks or months Best fit — receive, inspect, hold until the reveal Not built for long holds In-stock, local and regional retail, marketplace, compressed timeline Overkill — you pay to store what you could route Best fit — consolidate pickups, place on install day Long gap between purchase and install Warehouse holds it Book once the site is ready Client home ready on delivery day Adds a handling and delivery leg One booking, up to five stops, room-of-choice placement A lot of designers pay for a warehouse contract on projects that never needed one. When a Receiving Warehouse Earns Its Cost Four things make it the right call: freight-shipped custom and to-the-trade orders landing weeks apart, a client's home mid-renovation that can't take a carton, and a reveal where the whole value is that the client never sees a half-finished room. Early damage detection is the fourth — catching a cracked veneer on receipt instead of on install day can save the date. To-the-trade shipments usually arrive with no in-room service. The carrier drops a crated dining table at the curb or in the garage, marks it delivered, and leaves. Someone still has to uncrate it, inspect it, and hold it until the room is ready. Lugg is not a receiving warehouse and doesn't hold long-term storage. What it replaces is the coordination, not the building. How to Consolidate Multi-Vendor Deliveries Into One Route When the pieces are ready and the site is ready, the job is the route. A single Lugg booking allows up to five stops , so one crew can hit two showrooms, swing by a marketplace pickup , grab a piece waiting at the retail store , and drop everything at the client's home in one trip. New item in, old item out — you can add a donation or disposal stop in the same booking to clear what the redesign replaced. You pick the vehicle to the load — a cargo van for a few accent pieces, a box truck for a full living room — so you're not paying for space you don't use or squeezing a sectional into something too small. And because Lugg has real-time live tracking, you and the client both watch the same route move instead of sitting through a four-hour "delivery window." For designers juggling several projects in a week, that visibility is what protects the calendar. A real route looks like this. A designer closing out a smaller room books a van: two accent chairs from a showroom, a vintage sideboard off Facebook Marketplace, and a rug from a local shop, sequenced so the crew loads in pickup order and unloads in placement order at the client's home. A bigger project the same week takes a box truck — a sofa, dining set, and bed frame from two retail stops, dropped and placed room by room. Two bookings, two routes, and nobody sitting at a job site waiting on a carrier that said "sometime Thursday." What Room-of-Choice Delivery Should Cover on Install Day Threshold delivery drops your pieces at the door. Room-of-choice means they land where they're going — the sofa in the living room, the bed frame in the primary suite, the console against the right wall. You book the delivery to your install window — same-day when a piece comes in late, or scheduled up to 60 days out for a planned reveal — so the crew arrives when the room is ready and you're there to direct placement rather than fielding calls from a driver at the curb. The crew brings the blankets, straps, dollies, and stretch wrap, and can handle basic assembly and disassembly — a bed frame, a table, legs back onto a console. They place appliances in the room, but not electrical, plumbing or gas hookups, and anything torque-specific or warranty-sensitive should go to a technician. Every mover is background-checked, performance-monitored, holds a 4.7-plus rating to stay on the platform, and has prior furniture experience — which matters when they're carrying a client's $6,000 credenza up a staircase. What Designer Delivery Actually Costs Standard Lugg pricing is a base fare, per-minute labor that pauses during transit, and mileage between stops — with an upfront estimate before you book. There are no hourly minimums, so a 30-minute drop doesn't get billed as two hours the way a lot of task-based help does. Set that against a receiving-warehouse contract, which typically means monthly storage plus handling fees on both ends plus the delivery leg. On a long-lead custom project, that structure is worth every dollar. On a quick-turn room sourced locally, most of that spend is storage for pieces that were ready to go the day you bought them. Who's on the Hook When a Piece Gets Dinged Damage is the question designers actually lose sleep over, because a scratched dining table surfaces in front of the client. With direct-to-site vendor deliveries, damage often doesn't show up until install day, when it's too late to reorder. The warehouse model earns its keep here by inspecting on receipt — that's a real advantage of paying for one. When you route deliveries through Lugg instead, every booking is covered by the Damage Protection Guarantee, and the crew documents condition at pickup rather than leaving it a mystery until the reveal. If something does go wrong, Lugg works toward a damage-claim resolution in about three days. It's not a receiving warehouse's inspection-and-inventory system, but for locally sourced, quick-turn work, a covered route with a crew that checks pieces at the curb closes most of the gap the warehouse was there to close. Buy the Warehouse When the Project Earns It — Route the Rest Using a receiving warehouse by reflex is what costs you, including on projects that were only ever a pickup list and an install date. Long-lead, freight-shipped, custom work belongs in a warehouse. Locally sourced, quick-turn rooms belong on a route — consolidated into a single multi-stop delivery that lands room-of-choice on the day you actually need it. Set up a Lugg account , enter the addresses for your next install, and book the whole run in one go.

title: 8 Best Patent Analytics Software Tools in 2026 (Ranked)
summary: Compare eight patent analytics software tools by use case, source coverage, evidence quality, review controls, and the deliverables they produce.
body_text: Back to insights 8 Best Patent Analytics Software Tools in 2026 (Ranked) August 12, 2026 &AI Team Patent analytics software covers distinct jobs, from portfolio benchmarking and prior art retrieval to court intelligence and claim-level work product. Products may draw from overlapping patent data, yet their units of analysis, source coverage, review controls, and outputs differ sharply. We compare eight platforms across those dimensions, explain the job each one fits, and give patent litigators and in-house IP teams a practical framework for choosing software that reaches the required deliverable. Key takeaways Our pick for patent-litigation analysis and work product: &AI. Best for portfolio benchmarking: LexisNexis PatentSight+. Best for enriched global patent data: Clarivate Derwent Patent Analytics. Best for configurable search and landscapes: Questel Orbit Intelligence. Best free starting point: Google Patents. Before buying, assess source coverage, auditability, security, attorney controls, and the exact output your team needs. Patent analytics software comparison Patent litigators and in-house intellectual property (IP) teams need different tools at different stages of the work. Each “best for” label reflects a specific job because a search database, portfolio dashboard, and litigation-work-product platform cannot be reduced to one universal score. Rank and tool Best for Primary output Important boundary 1. &AI Patent-litigation analysis and work product Source-linked prior art results, invalidity and infringement analysis, claim charts, contentions, and editable exports We do not replace patent prosecution or drafting software, docketing systems, or judge-analytics platforms 2. LexisNexis PatentSight+ Portfolio benchmarking and patent-quality analytics Portfolio metrics, competitive benchmarks, technology landscapes, and strategic visualizations Portfolio metrics do not produce matter-specific claim mappings 3. Clarivate Derwent Patent Analytics Curated patent data and strategic landscapes Normalized portfolio views, dashboards, scores, landscapes, and reports Strategic analysis is not litigation work product 4. Questel Orbit Intelligence Configurable patent search, analysis, and reporting Search sets, graphs, landscapes, portfolio analysis, and reports Teams need to assess the exact data, interface, and handoffs required 5. IPRally AI-assisted prior art search and review Ranked patent results, review projects, classifications, and monitoring Relevant results still require legal analysis and source validation 6. Patlytics Broad AI-native patent workflows Search, portfolio analysis, claim construction, infringement and invalidity analysis, and claim charts Module depth and output controls can vary by workflow 7. Lex Machina Patent-litigation intelligence Court, judge, party, counsel, timing, motion, outcome, and damages analytics Litigation trends do not decide claim merits or create claim charts 8. Google Patents Free exploratory patent searching Search results, patent families, citations, classifications, and links to records No matter workflow, attorney approval gate, or litigation-ready output Start with the job and output “Patent analytics software” is an umbrella term. Some products analyze patent families and owners across a market. Others retrieve prior art, monitor court activity, or turn evidence into a claim chart. Six questions expose those differences: What sources does the product cover? Patents alone may be enough for a portfolio view but not for a litigation search that needs non-patent literature, archived web pages, standards, manuals, or product evidence. What is the unit of analysis? A patent family, company, technology cluster, claim limitation, accused product, case, and judge answer different questions. What output does the team receive? A dashboard, result list, alert, and editable invalidity chart are not substitutes. Can a reviewer trace every material conclusion to its source? Citations should open to the exact passage, figure, image, or record. Does the workflow preserve attorney control? The product should expose missing evidence and make review, revision, and approval visible. Does the system fit the buyer? Patent litigators, search professionals, R&D leaders, and portfolio strategists need different controls and handoffs. 1. &AI: best for patent-litigation analysis and work product Our product overview brings prior art search, claim charts, invalidity analysis, infringement detection, and business development into one patent-litigation workspace. Best for: Patent litigators and in-house IP teams that need to move from evidence discovery to attorney-reviewed work product. We rank &AI first for patent-litigation teams because our workspace connects parts of the workflow that general analytics platforms often leave separate. Teams can search patent and non-patent literature, product materials, and archived web sources; map evidence to individual claim limitations; develop invalidity or infringement positions; review citations; and export the work in editable formats. Our litigation-specific modules cover distinct but connected jobs: Our Prior Art Search searches patents, non-patent literature, product documentation, clinical-trial material, and archived web sources. Users can start from a patent, claim limitation, description, or figure. Our Invalidity Analysis supports Section 102, 103, and 112 analysis, including single-reference mappings, multi-reference combinations, visible coverage gaps, and draft contentions. Our Infringement Detection maps claim limitations to product evidence such as manuals, specifications, screenshots, teardowns, and video timestamps. Our Claim Charts keeps pinpoint source citations beside each limitation. Attorneys review and approve citations before they appear in exported work product. That evidence-to-output chain is why we rank our workspace first. Patent litigators rarely need one more dashboard. They need a defensible path from a source to a proposition, then into a chart, contention, memo, or other editable deliverable. We maintain controls relevant to confidential legal work, including SOC 2 Type II certification, zero-data-retention agreements with model providers, encryption in transit and at rest, single sign-on, and role-based access controls. Matter-specific requirements still determine whether those controls are sufficient. Where we are not the best fit: We do not replace patent prosecution or drafting software, a docketing system, or a general court-analytics platform. We are strongest when the output is patent-litigation analysis or work product. 2. LexisNexis PatentSight+: best for portfolio benchmarking PatentSight+ presents itself as a strategic patent-analysis platform for high-value portfolio decisions. Best for: IP strategy leaders comparing portfolio strength, competitive position, technology direction, or potential transaction targets. PatentSight+ is built around normalized patent-family and ownership data plus portfolio metrics. Its Patent Asset Index combines Technology Relevance and Market Coverage to compare the strength and reach of patent families and portfolios. The platform is useful when the question is strategic: Which companies lead a technology? Where is a portfolio gaining or losing strength? Which assets deserve maintenance, licensing, acquisition, or divestment review? PatentSight+ supports competitive benchmarking, technology landscapes, portfolio optimization, R&D analysis, licensing, and due diligence. Its value depends on the methodology matching the decision. Citation influence, geographic coverage, ownership normalization, and family definitions can illuminate a portfolio, but no portfolio score proves infringement, invalidity, or claim scope. Material findings should remain traceable to the underlying patents and current legal record. Where it is not the best fit: Choose a litigation-work-product platform when the deliverable is a limitation-level invalidity or infringement analysis rather than a portfolio benchmark. 3. Clarivate Derwent Patent Analytics: best for enriched data and strategic landscapes Derwent Patent Analytics centers its product page on portfolio insights and competitive intelligence from patent data. Best for: Patent professionals who need curated global patent data for portfolio, competitor, technology, and licensing analysis. Derwent Patent Analytics combines patent, citation, prosecution, company, and litigation data for strategic analysis. Its data foundation includes the Derwent World Patents Index, which groups inventions into families and adds normalized records and human-authored titles and summaries. The platform supports portfolio comparisons, technology landscapes, configurable scoring, dashboards, competitor monitoring, and reports. This makes it a strong option when messy names, ownership structures, family groupings, and multilingual patent records would otherwise distort the analysis. The data layer deserves the same scrutiny as the interface. Ask which fields are reported, normalized, inferred, or corrected; how often each source is updated; and what happens when an assignee, legal-status, or family record changes. Normalized analytics accelerate review, but official patent-office and court records remain the source of record for legal decisions. Where it is not the best fit: A strategic landscape or strength score does not replace source-linked claim analysis, an invalidity theory, or an evidence-of-use chart. 4. Questel Orbit Intelligence: best for configurable patent search and analysis Orbit Intelligence positions search and analytics together for work across the global patent database. Best for: Experienced patent searchers and analysts who want flexible queries, large-scale analysis, customizable graphs, and reusable reports. Orbit Intelligence combines patent search with analysis and visualization. Teams can adapt graphs to their reporting needs, analyze large result sets, compare portfolios and technology areas, and use patent-value indicators to support licensing, pruning, scouting, or project decisions. Orbit is a good fit when analysts want to move repeatedly between a search set and a landscape view without exporting every intermediate result. The ability to customize the analysis matters because a useful chart should reflect the buyer's taxonomy, markets, and decision rather than a vendor's default categories. Where it is not the best fit: Flexible search and graphs do not by themselves create an attorney-reviewed litigation position. A pilot should establish whether material results remain traceable to source records and move into the team's final work-product workflow without losing annotations or context. 5. IPRally: best for AI-assisted prior art search and review IPRally focuses its product overview on enterprise patent search, review, and classification. Best for: Patent and R&D teams that want a specialized AI search experience for prior art, freedom-to-operate review, monitoring, and patent classification. IPRally uses graph-based search trained on patent data. Its search options include free text, patent publication numbers, claim-like graph queries, Boolean fields, filters, and images. Review features include an AI assistant that can answer questions across one or multiple patents, project workspaces, relevance marking, comments, and portfolio classification. This makes IPRally attractive when the hardest part of the job is finding technically relevant patents despite different wording. Searchers can start from an invention description or known patent, refine results, and organize review without building a complex Boolean query first. Retrieval still needs a legal frame. USPTO examination guidance illustrates the distinction: Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) § 2131 says anticipation requires every claim element to be found expressly or inherently in a single reference, while MPEP § 2141 calls for factual findings and an articulated, reasoned basis for obviousness. A semantically close document is a candidate for review, not a legal conclusion. Compare the broader AI prior art search tools before choosing a search workflow. Where it is not the best fit: If the end product is an invalidity contention, infringement chart, or other litigation deliverable, downstream mapping, approval, and export belong in the evaluation alongside search relevance. 6. Patlytics: best for broad AI-native patent workflows Patlytics presents a broad AI patent platform intended to support several patent workflows. Best for: Teams evaluating one AI-native platform across several patent search, analysis, portfolio, and litigation jobs. Patlytics publishes a broad module set spanning patent and non-patent-literature search, portfolio analysis, freedom to operate, claim construction, infringement, invalidity, and claim charting. Its invalidity workflow, for example, includes prior art search, limitation-level charts, Section 103 combinations, Section 112 analysis, customizable contention templates, and Word or Excel exports. That breadth is useful for organizations trying to reduce handoffs across multiple patent workflows. It also makes module-level evaluation important. A strong portfolio view does not prove the depth of an invalidity chart, and a strong search experience does not prove the quality of an infringement export. Where it is not the best fit: Platform breadth alone is not a sufficient buying criterion. A useful evaluation runs the exact module with known sources, deliberately missing evidence, the team's template, and its security requirements. Correction time and reviewer effort matter alongside generation speed. 7. Lex Machina: best for patent-litigation intelligence Lex Machina centers its product page on actionable intelligence from structured litigation data. Best for: Litigation teams analyzing courts, judges, parties, law firms, counsel, case timing, motions, outcomes, damages, and market activity. Lex Machina turns docket and case information into litigation analytics. Its court, judge, counsel, party, and law-firm views support case strategy, competitive intelligence, business development, outside-counsel selection, and budgeting. Users can compare experience, timing to key milestones, motion patterns, resolutions, and damages, then inspect the underlying matters. This is a different job from patent-family analytics or claim mapping. Lex Machina helps answer questions such as how a judge has handled a motion, which firms appear in a venue, or how long a case may take. It does not decide whether a reference anticipates a claim or whether a product practices a limitation. Where it is not the best fit: Pair litigation intelligence with separate patent-evidence and work-product tools when the matter requires prior art, infringement evidence, claim construction, or a claim chart. 8. Google Patents: best free starting point Google Patents provides a free advanced-search interface with bibliographic and legal-status filters. Best for: Quick exploratory patent searches, family and citation research, classification research, and links to patent records. Google Patents is a free, browser-based starting point. Its advanced search supports keywords, Boolean syntax, title, abstract, claim and full-text fields, Cooperative Patent Classification codes, publication numbers, patent lists, and non-patent literature. It is useful for examining a known patent, exploring terminology, following citations, and building an initial search trail without a paid subscription. Free access is not the same as a complete legal workflow. Searchers must still document queries, establish family and legal-status information from authoritative records, preserve relevant sources, use multiple databases, and map evidence to the applicable legal standard. Where it is not the best fit: Google Patents does not provide matter permissions, structured attorney approvals, confidential collaboration, work-product templates, or litigation-ready exports. How to choose patent analytics software A polished demo can hide the failures that matter most. Run a bounded pilot against work your team understands. 1. Define the decision and required output Write down the decision, unit of analysis, source of record, final deliverable, owner, and reviewer. “Analyze this portfolio” is too broad. “Identify the strongest two Section 102 candidates, establish the support for each limitation, and produce an editable chart for independent attorney review” is a bounded assignment. 2. Match source coverage to the question Ask which patent offices, court sources, non-patent-literature collections, standards, product repositories, and archived websites are covered. Record update frequency, through-dates, excluded content, normalization rules, and links to original records. The forum can change the evidence boundary. An inter partes review challenge under 35 U.S.C. § 311(b) is limited to patents and printed publications under Sections 102 and 103. District-court analysis may also require product manuals, standards, source code, archived pages, videos, or other evidence. 3. Trace the entire evidence chain Follow one proposition from retrieval through the final deliverable. The source, date, passage, claim construction, reviewer comments, edits, and approval should survive every handoff. The Northern District of California Patent Local Rules illustrate why topic-level relevance is insufficient. Rules 3-1 and 3-3 require parties to identify where and how claim limitations appear in accused products or prior art and to state the relevant invalidity theories. The controlling requirements vary by venue and posture, but the software should make exact support and missing support visible. 4. Evaluate confidentiality and control Review which models and subprocessors receive matter data, whether inputs are retained or used for training, who can access a matter, where data is stored, how it is deleted, and what the vendor logs. Certifications help, but they do not answer every matter-specific question. A deliberately unsupported proposition belongs in the pilot. The system should expose the gap or route it to review rather than manufacture a confident answer. 5. Score a real-work pilot Build a benchmark with known references, hard negatives, ambiguous claims, recent records, missing sources, and your real output format. Score source coverage, retrieval, citation validity, proposition support, completeness, repeatability, reviewer time, correction time, and export usability separately. Set scale, revise, and stop thresholds before the results arrive. A missed reference, unsupported proposition, confidentiality problem, and formatting defect should not carry the same weight. body_text: False claims about Covid-19 vaccines and miscarriage are circulating online again, fueled by renewed debate over data collected during the early stages of the pandemic. One of the most widely repeated claims suggests that Covid-19 vaccination was associated with an 82% miscarriage rate. However, that figure comes from a flawed interpretation of an early vaccine safety study and does not represent the actual miscarriage risk among vaccinated pregnant women. The issue has resurfaced following the release of text messages from Dr. Anthony Fauci's former government phone. Republican Sens. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin and Rand Paul of Kentucky released messages as part of their investigation into the federal government's handling of the Covid-19 pandemic. Some of the messages discussed theoretical questions about vaccine safety during pregnancy. Those messages have since been used online to support claims that Covid-19 vaccines cause miscarriages. Medical experts say the interpretation is not supported by the broader body of scientific evidence. Where the 82% Figure Came From The controversy centers on a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine in April 2021. Researchers examined information from a vaccine safety monitoring system involving almost 4,000 women who received Covid-19 vaccines during the early months of the vaccine rollout. Among those participants, researchers identified 827 pregnancies with known outcomes at the time of the initial analysis. There were 712 live births, 104 spontaneous abortions, commonly referred to as miscarriages, and 11 other outcomes. Simply dividing 104 miscarriages by 827 completed pregnancies produces a figure of approximately 12.6%. Even that calculation required considerable caution because the study population and follow-up period had limitations. A correction published later in 2021 made the situation clearer. Researchers explained that the available information did not allow them to calculate a reliable miscarriage rate from those numbers. Many participants had not been followed long enough for their pregnancy outcomes to be known, meaning the 827 completed pregnancies could not appropriately serve as the denominator for the entire group. The researchers also pointed out an important statistical issue. About 700 of the completed pregnancies were already in their third trimester when vaccination occurred. Since most miscarriages happen earlier in pregnancy, those pregnancies could not simply be included or excluded without taking the timing of vaccination and pregnancy into account. How the Data Became Distorted Critics of Covid-19 vaccination have used the study's numbers in a different way. They exclude the approximately 700 third-trimester pregnancies and then calculate 104 miscarriages among the remaining 127 pregnancies. That calculation produces a figure close to 82%. The problem is that this number does not represent a miscarriage rate caused by vaccination. It uses a denominator that the researchers specifically said could not be used to calculate miscarriage risk. This is a crucial distinction when interpreting medical research. A percentage can look alarming while still being statistically meaningless if the underlying population is selected incorrectly. In this case, the 82% figure is not a finding from the study. It is the result of applying an inappropriate calculation to incomplete data. What Larger Studies Have Found The early study was never the final word on Covid-19 vaccination during pregnancy. Since 2021, researchers have accumulated substantially more information involving pregnant women who received Covid-19 vaccines. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, numerous studies have found no increased health risks for pregnant women or their babies associated with Covid-19 vaccination. The agency also says research indicates that vaccination during pregnancy can provide protection to both the mother and baby. Medical organizations specializing in pregnancy and infectious diseases have similarly continued to support vaccination during pregnancy based on the available evidence. Dr. Kevin Ault, an obstetrician and gynecologist, told CNN that the subject has been extensively studied and that a major increase in miscarriage risk would be extremely difficult to overlook after years of additional research. Dr. Brenna Hughes of the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine has also emphasized that the benefits of vaccination outweigh the potential risks based on the accumulated scientific literature. Covid-19 Infection Can Be Dangerous During Pregnancy Another important part of the discussion is the risk posed by Covid-19 infection itself. Pregnancy can increase the risk of serious complications from respiratory infections, and Covid-19 has been associated with severe illness, intensive care admissions and other adverse pregnancy outcomes. Experts therefore stress that evaluating a vaccine during pregnancy requires comparing its potential risks with the risks of remaining unprotected against the disease. According to specialists quoted by CNN, vaccination can reduce the risk of severe Covid-19 complications during pregnancy. The available evidence therefore does not support treating the vaccine as a greater threat to pregnancy than the infection itself. Why Medical Data Need Context The controversy illustrates how easily scientific statistics can be misunderstood or deliberately presented without context. A study may contain a number that appears straightforward, but understanding what that number means requires examining how participants were selected, how long they were followed and whether the comparison group or denominator is appropriate. That is especially important with pregnancy research. The probability of miscarriage changes throughout pregnancy, so researchers must consider the gestational age at vaccination and other factors when calculating risk. Removing participants from a calculation simply because their pregnancies had progressed further can produce a dramatically different percentage without demonstrating that the underlying medical risk has changed. For people trying to make decisions about vaccination during pregnancy, isolated statistics shared on social media can therefore be particularly misleading. Where to Find Reliable Information Pregnant people with questions about Covid-19 vaccination should discuss their individual circumstances with a qualified health professional. Medical societies and public health agencies can also provide information based on reviews of the broader scientific literature rather than a single disputed calculation. The central point is straightforward: the claim that Covid-19 vaccines cause an 82% miscarriage rate is not an accurate interpretation of the evidence. The figure comes from manipulating the denominator of an early study in a way that the researchers themselves said was inappropriate for estimating miscarriage risk. Years of additional research have provided a much larger evidence base. That broader literature has not shown that Covid-19 vaccination increases the risk of miscarriage. Sources CNN, reporting on the disputed miscarriage claim and the interpretation of the 2021 vaccine safety study. New England Journal of Medicine , early safety monitoring study of Covid-19 vaccination during pregnancy. US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, information and research on Covid-19 vaccination during pregnancy. Mayo Clinic, general information about miscarriage and its frequency. Disclaimer This article is for general informational and educational purposes only. It is a written summary based on the supplied source material and should not be considered medical advice, a diagnosis, or a recommendation for any individual. Health guidance can change as new evidence becomes available. Pregnant people should consult their doctor, midwife or other qualified healthcare professional for advice about vaccination and their personal circumstances.
